content.text: So essentially, in the limiting case, we are writing an alternative compiler backend to work with specific computational substrate?

items.text:
Yes. We’re building a **specialized compiler backend and runtime for a particular computational substrate**.

The authored Lean program specifies behavior. The compiler chooses how that behavior is realized through native integers, memory layouts, C control flow, SQLite tables and queries, and OS services. Changing the substrate would mean changing those representations and lowering rules while preserving the program’s observable behavior.

The scope extends beyond ordinary code generation because storage and effects are part of the program. It’s closer to compiling an entire application—including its data representation and execution machinery—than compiling individual functions.

The proof obligation is: **running the generated application produces the behavior specified by the source**, assuming the external substrate satisfies its stated contracts. Here, Clang, SQLite, and the OS are trusted through those contracts; our lowering and generated application remain obligations to prove.

That makes this a domain-specific compiler for an admitted fragment of Lean, rather than a replacement backend for arbitrary Lean programs.

content.text: So it both more general, and more specialized than writing the generic runtime.

items.text:
Yes, along different axes. **The generality moves into the compiler; the specialization moves into the generated runtime.**

A generic runtime fixes a set of mechanisms—object representations, dispatch, storage access—and lets many applications use them. This approach can derive those mechanisms from each application’s types, computations, and effects.

That gives it more freedom to produce different implementations, while each emitted implementation can be much narrower: exact layouts, direct control flow, specific queries, and only the machinery that application needs.

The qualification is that this doesn’t automatically support more source programs. Our admitted language may be narrower than what a generic runtime supports. The greater generality is in **which implementation decisions can vary across applications**, rather than necessarily in the range of applications accepted.
